title: Two Sum
problem: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.
approach: Use a hash map to store previously seen numbers and their indices. For each number, check whether target - number already exists.
interview_tip: Hashing can reduce the brute-force O(n²) solution to O(n).

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problem: Given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on the ith day, find the maximum profit that can be achieved by buying on one day and selling on a later day.
approach: Maintain the minimum price seen so far and calculate the maximum profit at every day.
interview_tip: Track the minimum value seen so far instead of checking every pair.

title: Contains Duplicate
problem: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice and false if every element is distinct.
approach: Use an unordered_set. While traversing the array, if an element already exists in the set, a duplicate is present.
interview_tip: A hash set provides average O(1) lookup.

title: Maximum Subarray
problem: Given an integer array nums, find the subarray with the largest sum and return its sum.
approach: Use Kadane's algorithm. Maintain the best sum ending at the current position and update the global maximum.
interview_tip: Kadane's algorithm is a must-know array pattern.

title: Product of Array Except Self
problem: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all elements of nums except nums[i].
approach: Build prefix products from the left and multiply them with suffix products from the right without using division.
interview_tip: Prefix and suffix techniques are useful when an answer depends on all elements except the current one.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
problem: Given an integer array nums, find a contiguous non-empty subarray that has the largest product and return the product.
approach: Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at each position because a negative number can turn the minimum into the maximum.
interview_tip: When multiplication and negative values are involved, track both maximum and minimum states.

title: Move Zeroes
problem: Given an integer array nums, move all zeroes to the end while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements.
approach: Use a pointer to place non-zero elements at the front, then fill the remaining positions with zeroes.
interview_tip: The slow-fast pointer pattern is common in array problems.

title: Majority Element
problem: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element. The majority element appears more than n/2 times.
approach: Use Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm. Maintain a candidate and count, cancelling different elements against the candidate.
interview_tip: Boyer-Moore is an important O(1) space voting technique.

title: 3Sum
problem: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that their sum is zero.
approach: Sort the array and fix one element. Use two pointers for the remaining two elements while skipping duplicates.
interview_tip: Sorting plus two pointers is a core pattern for pair and triplet problems.

title: Container With Most Water
problem: Given an integer array height, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container containing the most water.
approach: Start with pointers at both ends. Calculate the area and move the pointer with the smaller height.
interview_tip: When maximizing distance-based pair values, consider whether two pointers can eliminate impossible candidates.

title: Valid Palindrome
problem: Given a string s, determine if it is a palindrome considering only alphanumeric characters and ignoring cases.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

approach: Use two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing lowercase characters.
interview_tip: Two pointers are often the simplest solution for palindrome problems.

title: Valid Anagram
problem: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s and false otherwise.
approach: Count the frequency of each character in both strings and compare the counts.
interview_tip: Frequency counting is one of the most common string problem patterns.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problem: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
approach: Use a sliding window with a frequency array or hash map. Expand the right pointer and move the left pointer when a duplicate appears.
interview_tip: Sliding window is essential for substring and subarray problems with constraints.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problem: Given a string s and an integer k, you can replace at most k characters. Return the length of the longest substring containing the same letter after replacements.
approach: Maintain a sliding window and the frequency of its most common character. If window size minus maximum frequency exceeds k, shrink the window.
interview_tip: A useful sliding-window condition is window_size - most_frequent_count <= k.

title: Binary Search
problem: Given a sorted array of integers nums and an integer target, return the index of target if it exists, otherwise return -1.
approach: Maintain a search range using left and right pointers. Compare the middle element with the target and eliminate half of the search space.
interview_tip: Know both the standard binary search template and how to avoid integer overflow in mid calculation.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problem: Given an array nums sorted in ascending order and rotated at an unknown pivot, search for target and return its index.
approach: At every step one half of the array is guaranteed to be sorted. Determine which half is sorted and check whether the target belongs to that range.
interview_tip: In rotated binary search, first identify which half is sorted.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problem: Given a sorted array that has been rotated between 1 and n times, find the minimum element.
approach: Compare the middle element with the rightmost element to determine which half contains the minimum.
interview_tip: Binary search can locate a boundary or extremum, not just an exact target.

title: Reverse Linked List
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the reversed list.
approach: Use three pointers: previous, current, and next. Reverse each current node's pointer and move forward.
interview_tip: Always save curr->next before changing the pointer.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problem: Merge two sorted linked lists and return the head of the merged sorted list.
approach: Use a dummy node and repeatedly attach the smaller current node from the two lists.
interview_tip: Dummy nodes simplify linked-list insertion and merging.

title: Linked List Cycle
problem: Given the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list contains a cycle.

examples.input: head = [3,2,0,-4], tail connects to node index 1

approach: Use Floyd's slow and fast pointer algorithm. If the pointers meet, a cycle exists.
interview_tip: Floyd's cycle detection algorithm is a fundamental linked-list technique.

title: Middle of the Linked List
problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node.
approach: Use slow and fast pointers. Slow moves one step while fast moves two steps. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.
interview_tip: Slow-fast pointers can solve many linked-list problems in one pass.

title: Valid Parentheses
problem: Given a string containing parentheses, determine if the input string is valid. Every opening bracket must be closed by the same type of bracket in the correct order.
approach: Use a stack. Push opening brackets and ensure every closing bracket matches the top of the stack.
interview_tip: Stacks are ideal when the latest unmatched opening element must be processed first.

title: Min Stack
problem: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time.
approach: Maintain a second stack containing the minimum value at each stack level.
interview_tip: An auxiliary data structure can maintain additional state while preserving O(1) operations.

title: Daily Temperatures
problem: Given an array of daily temperatures, return an array where answer[i] tells how many days you have to wait after day i to get a warmer temperature.
approach: Use a decreasing monotonic stack of indices. When the current temperature is greater than the temperature at the stack top, resolve that previous day.
interview_tip: Monotonic stacks are useful for next greater/smaller element problems.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values.
approach: Use a queue for BFS. Process all nodes currently in the queue as one level before moving to the next level.
interview_tip: BFS with a queue is the standard approach for level-order traversal.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth.
approach: Use recursion. The depth of a node is one plus the maximum depth of its left and right subtrees.
interview_tip: Many tree problems can be expressed naturally using recursive subtree relationships.

title: Invert Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree and return its root.
approach: Recursively invert the left and right subtrees and then swap the two child pointers.
interview_tip: Think of tree recursion as solving the same problem independently for each subtree.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
problem: Given a binary search tree and two nodes p and q, find their lowest common ancestor.
approach: Use the BST ordering property. If both nodes are smaller, move left. If both are larger, move right. Otherwise the current node is the LCA.
interview_tip: Always look for properties of BSTs that can eliminate unnecessary traversal.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid binary search tree.
approach: Recursively maintain a valid range for each node. Every node must be strictly greater than its lower bound and smaller than its upper bound.
interview_tip: For BST validation, checking only immediate children is insufficient; maintain the full valid range.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problem: Given the root of a binary search tree, return the kth smallest value among all the node values.
approach: An inorder traversal of a BST visits nodes in sorted order. Stop when the kth node is visited.
interview_tip: Remember: inorder traversal of a BST produces values in sorted ascending order.

title: Merge Intervals
problem: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start, end], merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of non-overlapping intervals.
approach: Sort intervals by starting time. Iterate through them and merge the current interval with the last interval in the answer whenever they overlap.
space_complexity: O(n) excluding sorting space and output
interview_tip: Whenever a problem involves overlapping ranges or time intervals, consider sorting by starting time.

title: Insert Interval
problem: Given a collection of non-overlapping intervals sorted by starting time and a new interval, insert the new interval and merge if necessary.
approach: Add all intervals that end before the new interval. Merge all overlapping intervals with the new interval. Finally, add the remaining intervals.
interview_tip: Divide interval processing into three phases: before, overlapping, and after.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problem: Given an array of intervals, return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest non-overlapping.
approach: Sort intervals by ending time. Greedily select intervals that start at or after the ending time of the previously selected interval. Remove the rest.
interview_tip: For interval scheduling problems, sorting by ending time often leads to a greedy solution.

title: Meeting Rooms II
problem: Given an array of meeting time intervals, find the minimum number of conference rooms required.
approach: Sort meetings by starting time and maintain a min heap of ending times. Remove meetings that have already finished before assigning a room to the next meeting.
interview_tip: A min heap is useful when you need to efficiently track the earliest finishing task or meeting.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.
approach: Count frequencies using an unordered_map. Maintain a min heap of size k based on frequency.
time_complexity: O(n + m log k), where m is the number of distinct elements
interview_tip: Top K problems are classic candidates for a frequency map combined with a heap.

title: Group Anagrams
problem: Given an array of strings, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order.
approach: Sort each string to create a common key for all its anagrams. Store strings with the same key in an unordered_map.
time_complexity: O(n * k log k), where k is the maximum string length
interview_tip: Find a canonical representation when different inputs need to be grouped by equivalent properties.

title: Encode and Decode Strings
problem: Design an algorithm to encode a list of strings into one string and decode it back into the original list of strings.
approach: Prefix each string with its length followed by a delimiter. During decoding, read the length and extract exactly that many characters.
time_complexity: O(S), where S is the total number of characters
interview_tip: Length-prefix encoding avoids ambiguity when strings contain delimiters or special characters.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problem: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of continuous subarrays whose sum equals k.
approach: Maintain a running prefix sum. For every position, look for the frequency of prefixSum - k in a hash map.
interview_tip: Remember the equation: prefixSum[j] - prefixSum[i] = k. This is a fundamental prefix-sum pattern.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problem: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. Your algorithm must run in O(n) time.
approach: Insert all numbers into an unordered_set. Start counting only when the current number has no predecessor in the set.
interview_tip: Avoid sorting when the problem explicitly demands O(n). Hash sets can help identify sequence starting points.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problem: Given an m x n integer matrix, if an element is zero, set its entire row and column to zero. You must do it in place.
approach: Use the first row and first column as markers to indicate which rows and columns should be set to zero. Handle their original zero states separately.
interview_tip: Matrix problems often have optimized solutions that use the first row and column as auxiliary storage.

title: Spiral Matrix
problem: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order.
approach: Maintain four boundaries: top, bottom, left, and right. Traverse each boundary in clockwise order and shrink the boundaries after every traversal.
interview_tip: Carefully update matrix boundaries and check them before traversing the remaining rows or columns.

title: Rotate Image
problem: You are given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image. Rotate the image 90 degrees clockwise in place.
approach: First transpose the matrix by swapping matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]. Then reverse every row.
interview_tip: A 90-degree clockwise rotation can be achieved using transpose followed by reversing each row.

title: Jump Game
problem: Given an integer array nums, where each element represents the maximum jump length from that position, determine if you can reach the last index.
approach: Maintain the farthest reachable index. If the current index exceeds the farthest reachable index, return false.
interview_tip: Greedy algorithms often work by maintaining the farthest reachable position or the best choice so far.

title: Jump Game II
problem: Given an integer array nums, return the minimum number of jumps required to reach the last index. You can assume the last index is always reachable.
approach: Treat the current jump range as a level. Track the farthest index reachable within this range. When reaching the end of the current range, increment the jump count.
interview_tip: Think of greedy jump ranges as levels of BFS. Each level represents one jump.

title: Coin Change
problem: You are given an integer array coins representing coin denominations and an integer amount. Return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount. If it cannot be made, return -1.
approach: Use bottom-up dynamic programming. Let dp[i] represent the minimum coins needed to make amount i. Try every coin denomination.
time_complexity: O(amount * n), where n is the number of coin denominations
interview_tip: Define the DP state clearly before writing transitions. Here dp[i] represents the minimum coins required for amount i.

title: Climbing Stairs
problem: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. You can climb either 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.
approach: Use dynamic programming. The number of ways to reach step n equals the sum of ways to reach n-1 and n-2.
interview_tip: Recognize Fibonacci-style recurrence relations in counting problems.

title: House Robber
problem: You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. You cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return the maximum amount of money you can rob.
approach: At every house, choose between skipping it or robbing it and adding its money to the best result from two houses before.
interview_tip: For non-adjacent selection problems, consider the two choices: take the current element or skip it.

title: Unique Paths
problem: A robot is located at the top-left corner of an m x n grid. It can move only down or right. Return the number of unique paths to reach the bottom-right corner.
approach: Use a one-dimensional DP array. The number of paths to a cell equals the paths from the top plus the paths from the left.
interview_tip: Grid DP problems often use transitions from the top and left cells.

title: Combination Sum
problem: Given an array of distinct integers candidates and a target integer target, return all unique combinations where the chosen numbers sum to target. You may use the same number unlimited times.
approach: Use backtracking. At each index, either choose the current candidate again or move to the next candidate. Stop when the remaining target becomes zero or negative.
space_complexity: O(target / min(candidates)) recursion depth, excluding output
interview_tip: In backtracking, distinguish between reusing the current element and moving to the next element.

title: Subsets
problem: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets, also known as the power set.
approach: Use backtracking. At every index, make two choices: include the current element or exclude it.
space_complexity: O(n) auxiliary recursion space, excluding output
interview_tip: Subsets are a fundamental include-or-exclude backtracking pattern. An array of n elements has 2^n subsets.

title: Permutations
problem: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all possible permutations.
approach: Use backtracking with a visited array. Select an unused element, add it to the current permutation, recursively continue, and backtrack.
interview_tip: Subsets use include/exclude decisions, while permutations require tracking which elements have already been used.

title: Word Search
problem: Given an m x n grid of characters and a string word, return true if the word exists in the grid. Adjacent cells must be horizontally or vertically neighboring, and the same cell cannot be used more than once.
approach: Try starting DFS from every cell matching the first character. Explore four directions while marking visited cells temporarily. Backtrack after each attempt.
time_complexity: O(m * n * 3^L) for L > 1, as the first move can have four choices and subsequent moves at most three
space_complexity: O(m * n + L) including visited storage and recursion
interview_tip: Always restore the visited state during backtracking. Forgetting to unmark a cell can cause incorrect results.

title: Number of Islands
problem: Given an m x n grid of '1's representing land and '0's representing water, return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.
approach: Traverse every cell. Whenever an unvisited land cell is found, increment the island count and run DFS to mark the entire connected component as visited.
interview_tip: Connected component problems are commonly solved using DFS, BFS, or Disjoint Set Union.

title: Clone Graph
problem: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the graph.

examples.output: A deep copy of the original graph

approach: Use DFS and an unordered_map to map each original node to its cloned node. This prevents creating duplicate clones and handles cycles.
interview_tip: When cloning graph structures containing cycles, maintain a mapping of original nodes to cloned nodes.

title: Course Schedule
problem: There are numCourses courses labeled from 0 to numCourses - 1. Given prerequisite pairs, determine if it is possible to finish all courses.
approach: Use Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting. Build a directed graph and calculate indegrees. Process nodes with indegree zero using a queue. If all nodes are processed, there is no cycle.
interview_tip: Topological sorting is useful for dependency resolution and detecting cycles in directed graphs.

title: Graph Valid Tree
problem: Given n nodes labeled from 0 to n - 1 and a list of undirected edges, determine whether these edges form a valid tree.
approach: A valid undirected tree must have exactly n-1 edges and be connected. Check the edge count, then run DFS to verify connectivity.
interview_tip: For an undirected graph, a tree must be both connected and acyclic. Having exactly n-1 edges plus connectivity guarantees both.

title: Network Delay Time
problem: You are given a directed weighted graph with n nodes numbered from 1 to n. Find the time it takes for a signal sent from node k to reach all nodes. Return -1 if some nodes cannot be reached.
approach: Use Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm with a min heap. Calculate shortest distances from the source to every node and return the maximum distance.
interview_tip: Dijkstra is suitable for shortest paths when edge weights are non-negative. Use Bellman-Ford when negative edges need to be supported.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problem: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. It is the kth largest element in sorted order, not the kth distinct element.
approach: Maintain a min heap of size k. Insert every element and remove the smallest element whenever the heap size exceeds k.
interview_tip: For Kth largest or smallest problems, a heap of size k is a common solution. Quickselect can achieve average O(n) time.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problem: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of sizes m and n respectively, return the median of the two sorted arrays. The overall runtime complexity should be O(log(m+n)).
approach: Binary search on the smaller array to find a partition such that all elements on the left are smaller than or equal to all elements on the right. Use the partition sizes to calculate the median.
interview_tip: This is an important advanced binary search problem. Focus on understanding the partition conditions rather than memorizing the code.

title: LRU Cache
problem: Design a data structure that follows the Least Recently Used (LRU) cache policy. Implement get(key) and put(key, value), both in O(1) average time.

examples.input: LRUCache cache = new LRUCache(2); put(1,1); put(2,2); get(1); put(3,3); get(2)

approach: Use a doubly linked list to maintain usage order and an unordered_map to locate nodes in O(1) average time. The most recently used node stays near the head, and the least recently used node stays near the tail.
time_complexity: O(1) average per get and put
interview_tip: LRU Cache is a classic system-design-oriented DSA question. Understand why a hash map alone or a queue alone cannot efficiently implement all required operations.
